name: Logooli
sweep_summary: Logooli (logo1258) is not in the catalog. The five sweep items are one comparative thesis (Philippson 1991, Paris 5: ~30 East African Bantu languages on a tonal-to-penultimate-stress continuum; full text not online, theses.fr 'accessible: non', abstract read; Logooli membership in the sample unverified; medium priority for print acquisition) and four bibliographic variants of one paper, Goldsmith 'Tone and Accent in Llogoori' (AAP 25, 1991 = Joy of Grammar 1992, DOI 10.1075/z.55.07gol paywalled), read in full from the author's open scan at people.cs.uchicago.edu. Goldsmith describes Logooli as a tone language (H/L/toneless, downstep, syllable TBU, contrastive length) and posits an abstract quantity-sensitive metrical foot (first syllable extrametrical, iambic foot at left edge of stem) that governs where grammatical High tones dock in the Present Continuous and Middle Future; he states explicitly that there is no phonetic evidence of stress or rhythm. So the item is prosody-but-not-word-stress, not a stress-placement source. Additional open Logooli phonology read as controls: Odden 2019 (Loquens, geminate blockage), Odden 2021 (JUL, substance-free segmental phonology: 'Tone and vowel length do not figure into the present analysis'), Pak 2019 (Florida Linguistics Papers, grammatical tone, adopts Goldsmith's grid) — none mentions word stress or penultimate lengthening. Not obtainable online: Leung 1986/1991 Cornell 'The tonal phonology of Llogoori' (print only; Goldsmith's data source), Odden 2018 'Tonal melodies in the Logoori verb' (Chicago, paywalled), Appleby 1943 Luragoli grammar, Gudahi 2003 (Hathi search-only). No first-hand word-stress statement for Logooli was found; best_new_statement found=false. searches were done through Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (rate-limited), HAL, archive.org, theses.fr and direct site fetches.

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John A. (1992). Tone and Accent in Llogoori. In Brentari, Larson & MacLeod (eds.), The Joy of Grammar. A festschrift in honor of James D. McCawley, 73-94. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
sources.quote: The particular conclusion we draw is that Llogoori has developed a quantity-sensitive accentual system quite similar to the familiar quantity-sensitive pattern found in Latin or in English, a pattern in which vowel length determines syllable weight. [...] the present analysis adds to a growing body of literature that supports the position that metrical structure plays a role in the organization of language in a large number of cases in which there is no phonetic evidence of alternating stress or overt rhythm.
sources.note: Llogoori is described as a tone language (H/L, toneless morphemes, downstep, syllable as TBU; p. 2). The 'accent' of the title is an abstract metrical grid (a single quantity-sensitive iambic foot at the left edge of the verb stem, first syllable extrametrical in the Middle Future) that determines where a tense-specific High tone docks in two tenses (Present Continuous, Middle Future); Goldsmith states explicitly that there is no phonetic evidence of stress or rhythm. No statement of where phonetic word stress falls. Same text as the 1991 AAP article; read from the author's open scan, the Ben…

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John Anton (1991). Tone and accent in Llogori. Afrikanistische Arbeitspapiere (AAP) 25: 7-30.
sources.quote: For the practicing accentologist [...] the pattern is a clear one: it is the Latin stress rule, viewed through a mirror. Scanning rightward from the beginning, rather than leftward from the end as in Latin, we skip the first syllable, and then assign an accent to the next syllable (the second) if it is heavy, and skip it if it is light, assigning accent to the following syllable [...] Metrical theory informs us that the proper statement is: (1) assign extrametrical status to the first syllable; (2) assign a Q-sensitive iambic foot to the left end of the stem
sources.note: Original AAP version of the same paper (Pak 2019 cites it as AAP 25: 7-30). The 'accent' is a grid used to place grammatical High tones in two verb tenses, built on Leung's (1986/1991) Llogoori verb-tone data; it is tone assignment, not phonetic stress. No statement of word-stress location.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. [...] on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.note: Comparative typology of the tone/accent systems of ~30 East African Bantu languages, ranging from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili); the abstract does not say whether Logooli is in the sample, so what it says about Logooli specifically is unknown. theses.fr marks the thesis 'accessible: non' (no online full text); HAL search returned nothing; library-print-only (Sudoc).
